title: Sub-row-group scan morsels for tables with few row groups
hypothesis: Parallel table scans hand out one whole row group (~122k rows) per task (RowGroupCollection::NextParallelScan, non-verify path), and DataTable::MaxThreads returns total_rows/row_group_size+1. A table that fits in one row group is therefore scanned by one thread. In q02 the supplier scan (100k rows, projects 4 string columns, the optional IN filter is used only for zonemap pruning) takes 0.04s in the profile and 0.02s when run alone. That is single-threaded time on the critical path of an ~80ms query, because it feeds a CTE and a hash-join build. The part scan (2M rows = ~17 row groups over 8 threads) also balances poorly: 3 waves, the last one 1/8 full, with an expensive suffix() LIKE filter. Handing out sub-row-group morsels when the table has few row groups compared with the thread count would let small scans with heavy columns or expensive filters use every thread.
plan: In src/storage/table/row_group_collection.cpp RowGroupCollection::NextParallelScan, generalise the existing verify_parallelism branch, which already advances state.vector_index and computes max_row for one vector. Pick a morsel size in vectors: when the collection has fewer row groups than about 2x TaskScheduler::NumberOfThreads(), use max(1, ceil(row_group_vectors / per-thread share)) vectors, with a floor of e.g. 8 vectors (16k rows); otherwise keep the whole row group. Advance vector_index by that many vectors and add the morsel's rows (not the whole group) to processed_rows. The morsel size can be computed once in InitializeParallelScan and stored in ParallelCollectionScanState (src/include/duckdb/storage/table/scan_state.hpp), so ordering by batch_index stays monotonic. In src/storage/data_table.cpp DataTable::MaxThreads, return the matching number of morsels so the scan source actually launches enough threads. Keep the verify_parallelism behaviour (1 vector). InitializeScanInRowGroup(…, vector_index, max_row) -> RowGroup::InitializeScanWithOffset already supports offsets.
expected_gain: q02: the supplier scan goes from ~20-40ms single-threaded to ~5ms, and the part scan balances better. Estimate 15-30% on q02.
generality: Any scan of a small or medium table (< ~1M rows, or a row-group count not a multiple of the thread count) with wide string columns or expensive filters: dimension-table scans that feed joins or CTEs, and small-table aggregations. Large-table scans are unchanged (the condition does not trigger). Tiny tables may pay a little task overhead; the floor bounds it.
risk: Medium-low. The verify_parallelism path already exercises sub-row-group scans, so correctness paths (deletes, updates, zonemap checks per morsel, batch_index ordering for order-preserving sinks) are tested. Watch the progress-bar processed_rows accounting, and check that row-group-level zonemap pruning and checkpoint/row_id logic do not assume vector_index == 0.

title: Execute tiny dynamic IN filters in the scan instead of zonemap-only
hypothesis: PushInFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp) wraps the IN list from a small build side (<= dynamic_or_filter_threshold) in an OptionalFilter, so it is used only for zonemap pruning. In q02 the supplier scan emits 97,542 rows although only 20,051 match s_nationkey IN (5 values), so all 4 string columns are fetched and decompressed for 5x more rows than needed, then probed into the hash join. Running the IN filter on rows when the list is very small (e.g. <= 8 values) and the column is a numeric key would let the scan filter first and fetch the other columns only for qualifying rows.
plan: In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::PushInFilter (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp), when the unique list is small (e.g. <= 8) and the type is integral, push a SelectivityOptionalFilter (as the BF does, so it disables itself when it is not selective) instead of a zonemap-only OptionalFilter. Check how SelectivityOptionalFilter (src/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.cpp) runs a child filter row-wise.
expected_gain: q02: the supplier scan string fetch drops by ~5x; a few ms. Smaller than the morsel issue, but it compounds with it.
generality: Star joins where a filtered tiny dimension (a handful of keys) is probed by a medium or large table with wide payload columns. Could add cost when the IN is not selective; the selectivity guard mitigates this.
risk: Low-medium; the filter is semantically redundant with the join, so correctness is safe if NULL handling matches (the IN list excludes NULLs and inner-join semantics drop them anyway; this must not be applied for joins that keep NULL probe rows).

title: Sparse Select for BitPacking segments (decode only selected rows)
hypothesis: In q02 the partsupp probe scan is the largest single cost: 0.30s CPU summed over threads (about 37ms per thread at 8 threads, out of 71ms total). I measured its parts in isolation, hot: a plain 8M-row ps_partkey scan costs 0.02s; ps_partkey with the BF filter costs 0.08s (the BF hash+probe is about 7ns/row, already tight in bloom_filter.cpp); adding the two payload columns ps_suppkey and ps_supplycost raises it to 0.30s. Only about 1% of rows survive the BF (73k of 8M, about 18 rows per 2048-row vector), yet the payload columns cost about as much as a full 3-column scan (0.14s). The cause is in StandardColumnData::Select (src/storage/table/standard_column_data.cpp:103). It uses a specialised segment select only when the compression function has `select`. Only dict_fsst and constant implement it. BitPacking (src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp, GetBitpackingFunction) does not, so ColumnData::Select falls back to Scan (decode all 2048 values) plus Slice. Both payload columns are BitPacking with Constant validity, and Constant validity already has ConstantSelectValidity. So adding a bitpacking select is the only missing piece for the fast path.
plan: In src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp add template<class T> BitpackingSelect(ColumnSegment&, ColumnScanState&, idx_t vector_count, Vector &result, const SelectionVector &sel, idx_t sel_count), modelled on FSSTStorage::Select (fsst.cpp:713). It writes result_data[i] = value at row sel.get_index(i) for i < sel_count (flat result). It must leave the BitpackingScanState advanced by exactly vector_count rows, as a scan would. (1) Dense case (sel_count * 4 > vector_count), or the current metadata group is DELTA_FOR: decode the vector with BitpackingScanPartial<T> into a scratch buffer of STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE T held lazily in the scan state, then gather through sel. This costs the same as today, so it cannot regress. (2) Sparse case: walk the selected indices in ascending order (sel is ascending in scans) and keep a cursor `pos`. For each idx call scan_state.Skip(segment, idx - pos). Skip is O(1) for CONSTANT, CONSTANT_DELTA and FOR, crossing metadata groups by pointer arithmetic. Then read the single value the way BitpackingFetchRow does. Handle the case current_group_offset == BITPACKING_METADATA_GROUP_SIZE by calling LoadNextGroup first, as BitpackingScanPartial does. Cache the last unpacked 32-value algorithm group pointer so that neighbouring rows are not unpacked twice. For a DELTA_FOR group, Skip decodes and keeps current_delta_offset, so it stays correct, just not faster; the value is decoded the same way Skip's loop does. At the end call Skip(vector_count - pos). Register it in GetBitpackingFunction by setting `bitpacking.select = BitpackingSelect<T>;`, the same way dict_fsst.cpp:294 sets `res.select`. Check that the select function pointer signature matches compression_function.hpp. Run the bitpacking tests under test/sql/storage/compression/bitpacking/, plus selective-filter queries on persisted tables.
expected_gain: q02: payload-column cost in the partsupp scan drops from about 0.22s to about 0.03s CPU, so the scan goes from 0.30s to about 0.11s. That is roughly 15-25% of q02 wall time, because this scan is the critical path of the probe pipeline.
generality: Any persisted-table scan where a pushed filter (constant comparison, bloom-filter/IN join filter, LIKE) keeps a small fraction of each vector and the projected columns are bitpacked integers, decimals or dates. That is very common: selective joins into fact tables, TPC-H/TPC-DS-style payload columns. Dense selections use the old decode-then-gather path, so the only possible slowdown is the extra branch per vector.
risk: Medium-low. The bitpacking scan state must end up exactly where a full Scan would have left it, including metadata-group crossing and DELTA_FOR's current_delta_offset. A mistake gives wrong values for later vectors, but the bitpacking test suite and the hidden result checks should catch that. Falling back for DELTA_FOR and dense selections keeps the new code to the simple random-access modes.

title: Real-row execution of tiny dynamic IN filters
hypothesis: Carried over from the backlog. The supplier scan emits 96k rows where about 20k match s_nationkey IN (5 keys), because PushInFilter makes a zonemap-only OptionalFilter. In isolation the hot 7-column supplier scan costs 0.05s CPU at 8 threads against 0.01s at 1 thread. Scanning only 20% of the string columns through Select (FSST has select) would cut its cost.
plan: In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::PushInFilter (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp), for an integral key and an IN list of 8 values or fewer on an inner or semi join, wrap the IN filter in a SelectivityOptionalFilter (src/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.cpp) instead of a plain OptionalFilter, so it runs on rows and switches itself off when it is not selective. Note that RowGroup::CheckZonemap (row_group.cpp:626) marks every filter of type OPTIONAL_FILTER as always-true; check which filter_type SelectivityOptionalFilter reports.
expected_gain: q02: a few ms on the supplier branch (the CTE side).
generality: Star joins with a tiny filtered dimension probed by a wider table. The selectivity guard limits the downside.
risk: Low-medium; must not apply to joins that keep NULL or unmatched probe rows.

title: Compact sparse filtered scan output into fuller chunks within a morsel
hypothesis: In q02 the partsupp scan with the pushed bloom filter emits 73,008 rows out of 8M, which is about 18 rows per 2048-row vector. TableScanFunc (table_scan.cpp:316) returns every non-empty vector as its own DataChunk, so about 3,900 tiny chunks go through the pipeline. The first hash-join probe (p_partkey) shows 0.02-0.03s cumulative for only 73k probe rows. That is per-chunk overhead (hashing setup, ScanStructure init, operator dispatch), not per-row work. Measured with threads=8 hot: the 1-column BF scan is 0.06s and the HJ probe 0.01-0.02s, while a full unfiltered 3-column scan of partsupp takes only 1.6ms wall. Downstream joins are CachingPhysicalOperators and already coalesce their outputs, so the first operator after a selective scan is the one that pays. E0002 (a faster BitPacking select) showed no official gain, which suggests decode is not the bottleneck. Per-chunk overhead is the next suspect.
plan: In the parallel DuckTableScanState::TableScanFunc (src/function/table/table_scan.cpp, around line 316), when the scan has table filters and storage.Scan returns a chunk with 0 < size < STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/8, do not return it straight away. Copy it into a per-local-state buffer DataChunk of the output types (add a `DataChunk compact_buffer` to TableScanLocalState, initialised lazily with output.GetTypes()). Keep calling storage.Scan for the same morsel only (do NOT call NextParallelScan while the buffer is non-empty, so batch-index and insertion-order semantics are kept). Append each result with DataChunk::Append. Stop when the buffer holds >= STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/2 rows, when the next chunk would overflow STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE (in that case emit the buffer and keep the pending chunk for the next call, or simply stop before appending a chunk that does not fit), or when the morsel is exhausted (Scan returns 0). Then output.Move/Reference the buffer. If a chunk of size >= STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/8 arrives while the buffer is empty, return it unchanged (fast path, no copy). Handle the CanRemoveFilterColumns path by compacting after ReferenceColumns, and skip compaction for is_create_index. Keep the TASK_EXECUTOR async return logic unchanged: only return HAVE_MORE_OUTPUT/FINISHED after the buffer has been flushed. Verify that row-id/virtual columns come through Append correctly, and that the DataTable scan state lifetimes stay valid: strings are deep-copied by Append into the buffer's own heap.
expected_gain: q02: about 0.02-0.03s cumulative CPU on the first probe after the partsupp scan, plus less pipeline dispatch overhead. Estimated 4-8% wall. Also helps the supplier and part scans when they are selective (part: 8,061 of 2M rows).
generality: Any query whose table scan has a selective pushed filter (static predicates, bloom/IN join filters, LIKE) feeding joins, aggregates or projections. That is common in star-schema and TPC-H/DS style workloads. Queries could get slower when filters keep roughly 5-12% of rows (the copy cost of Append, including string deep-copies, without much overhead saved). The 1/8-vector trigger limits this. Scans without filters are unaffected.
risk: Medium-low. Correctness depends on not crossing morsel boundaries (batch index/order preservation) and on properly flushing the buffer at the end of the morsel and the scan. Wrong async-mode handling could drop or duplicate rows. The copy of string columns adds some cost.

title: Row-level execution of small dynamic IN filters behind a selectivity guard
hypothesis: Fresh profile of q02.m0 (8 threads): the supplier TABLE_SCAN is the most expensive operator, at 0.07s cumulative. It emits 96,066 rows with 7 projected columns (FSST s_name/s_phone/s_comment, uncompressed s_address), but only 20,051 survive the next hash join on s_nationkey = n_nationkey, whose build side is 5 nation rows. JoinFilterPushdownInfo::PushInFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:720-759) pushes the 5-key IN list wrapped in a plain OptionalFilter. OptionalFilter::FilterSelection (optional_filter.cpp:23) returns scan_count, so the list is only used for zonemaps and never on rows. The min/max range [min_key, max_key] is pushed as a SelectivityOptionalFilter, but it covers nearly the whole domain and filters nothing. Because no row-level filter is selective, RowGroup::Scan decompresses every string column for all rows. If the IN list ran on rows, the scan would filter s_nationkey first and then use the compression Select path for the remaining columns (FSSTStorage::Select exists, fsst.cpp:791) on about 20% of the rows. That cuts string decode and copy by about 5x, and the s_suppkey join and CTE materialisation would also get pre-filtered input.
plan: 1) In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::PushInFilter (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp), when in_list.size() <= a small constant (e.g. 16), wrap the InFilter in a SelectivityOptionalFilter instead of OptionalFilter. Use a new threshold constant in selectivity_optional_filter.hpp, e.g. IN_FILTER_THRESHOLD = 0.5f with check_n around 30, so it switches itself off when more than half the rows pass. Larger lists keep the current zonemap-only OptionalFilter. 2) ColumnSegment::FilterSelection (src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp:405) has no IN_FILTER case and would hit the 'unsupported type' InternalException at line 620. Add a case for TableFilterType::IN_FILTER. For integral and other fixed-width physical types, take the IN values into a small typed array once, then loop over the selection keeping rows that are valid and equal to any value (linear scan over k <= 16). Other types fall back to a generic Value-compare loop, or the wrapper is skipped for non-numeric types. Check that TableFilterState::Initialize gives IN_FILTER a usable state; it should be the default state. Alternative if (2) is messy: have the child be an ExpressionFilter over in_filter->ToExpression(BoundReferenceExpression), since EXPRESSION_FILTER is already supported in FilterSelection. Do NOT use ConjunctionOrFilter: its OR merge is quadratic per vector. 3) Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the supplier scan cardinality drops from about 96k to about 20k rows and that results match.
expected_gain: q02: supplier scan 0.07s down to about 0.02-0.03s cumulative, plus less work in the s_suppkey join (0.02s) and the CTE. The supplier branch feeds the CTE on the critical path, so expect roughly 5-10% wall (2-5ms of 45ms).
generality: Any equality join whose build side is a small set of keys (a filtered dimension with at most 16 distinct keys) probing a wider table with payload columns: star and snowflake joins with dimension filters (region/nation/category/date-month style). Queries where the IN list is not selective pay for about 30 vectors of checks, then the guard turns it off. Scans with no extra payload columns gain little. The join already pushes a row-level min/max SelectivityOptionalFilter on the same probe column, so the join types that receive pushed filters are already ones where row-level filtering is safe.
risk: Low-medium. Correctness: the IN list comes only from join keys and excludes NULLs (the ContainsNull check already returns early), so for joins where min/max is already applied on rows, dropping non-matching probe rows earlier is safe. Main risks: a missing IN_FILTER case in some other row-filter path (check that any switch on filter_type reached from the scan handles IN_FILTER, e.g. ColumnData::Filter / FiltersNullValues / ConstantFun::FiltersNullValues), and type mismatch between the in_list values (already cast to the storage type) and the vector's physical type.

title: Raise selectivity ratio required to materialize a common multi-table subplan
hypothesis: In q02, CommonSubplanOptimizer turns supplier⋈nation⋈region into a materialized CTE (__common_subplan_1), which both the outer query and the decorrelated min() subquery read. Measured hot, 8 threads, same session, 3 runs each: default 68.1 / 68.5 ms; with SET disabled_optimizers='common_subplan' 47.1 / 51.4 / 52.9 ms, about -25%. Computing the subplan on its own hot costs only about 5 ms, so recomputing it twice costs far less than materializing it does. Materializing costs a full pipeline barrier (CTE child meta-pipeline -> CTE_SCAN build pipeline -> partsupp probe), a copy of all 7 wide string columns, and the loss of the direct table-scan build sides and dynamic join-filter pushdown through the CTE. The rule is IsSelectiveMultiTablePlan (src/optimizer/common_subplan_optimizer.cpp:975). It materializes when est_card <= 2048 or est_card < max_base_card / CARDINALITY_RATIO with ratio 2. Here est_card = 19,230 and max base = 100,000 (ratio 5.2), so only a weakly selective subplan gets materialized. Materializing pays off when the shared subplan is much smaller than the scans it saves. At 2-8x reduction, recomputing in parallel pipelines is cheaper.
plan: In src/optimizer/common_subplan_optimizer.cpp, CommonSubplanFinder::IsSelectiveMultiTablePlan: raise CARDINALITY_RATIO from 2 to 8, so a non-aggregate multi-table subplan above 2048 rows is materialized only when its estimated output is below 1/8 of its largest base table. Leave CARDINALITY_THRESHOLD (2048) and the EndsInAggregateOrDistinct path in ShouldMaterialize unchanged. Verify with EXPLAIN q02.m0 that no __common_subplan CTE remains, that the result matches, and run bench. If the gain is not there, check whether the plan without the CTE differs in join order (EXPLAIN with the optimizer disabled). If it is, the gain comes from that rather than from the barrier, so record which.
expected_gain: q02: about -20 to -25% hot (measured 68 -> 50 ms with the optimizer disabled). The ratio is scale-invariant, and the plan does not depend on the region literal (the estimate is the same for any region).
generality: Helps any query with a repeated join subplan that is only weakly selective (2-8x reduction), for example correlated-subquery decorrelation over a dimension join (TPC-H Q2 shape, other dimension⋈dimension repeats). Strongly selective subplans (e.g. a Q11-style partsupp⋈supplier⋈nation with one nation, ~25x) and aggregate or distinct subplans still get materialized. Could be slower when a weakly selective subplan scans a very large table and recomputing it is expensive.
risk: Low for correctness: it only changes whether an existing, tested rewrite fires, and the result with the rewrite off is the original plan. Moderate performance risk on hidden queries whose 2-8x selective common subplans are expensive to recompute.

title: Rewrite correlated MIN/MAX scalar subquery over a subset of the outer join into a window aggregate
hypothesis: Hot measurements (8 threads, SF10): the q02 outer 5-way join with its full projection and TopN takes about 30ms, and the full q02 takes about 47ms. So about 17-20ms goes to the decorrelated min() subquery: the LEFT_DELIM_JOIN materialises the outer result, the RHS rescans all 8M partsupp rows (with a BF from the DELIM_GET keys, which costs about 9ms like the outer partsupp scan), probes the supplier CTE again, hash-aggregates by p_partkey and joins back. I hand-wrote the window form, `SELECT * FROM (SELECT ..., min(ps_supplycost) OVER (PARTITION BY p_partkey) m FROM <outer join>) WHERE ps_supplycost = m ORDER BY ... LIMIT 100`. It returns the same result in about 36ms hot against 47ms, so the second partsupp scan, the delim machinery and the CTE barrier all go away. This is the classic WinMagic unnesting: when the subquery's FROM tables and predicates are a subset of the outer query's, and the extra outer tables are tied to that subset only through the correlated columns, then agg over the subquery equals agg OVER (PARTITION BY the correlated outer columns) over the outer rows. For MIN and MAX this holds even if extra-table rows duplicate the partition.
plan:
In Binder::PlanFilter (src/planner/binder/query_node/plan_select_node.cpp:11), before PlanSubqueries, call a new helper, e.g. TryRewriteSubqueryToWindow(condition, root), in a new file src/planner/subquery/subquery_to_window.cpp or in plan_subquery.cpp. Steps:
(1) Split the condition into AND conjuncts. Find exactly one conjunct `colref = BoundSubqueryExpression` (either side) with subquery_type SCALAR and IsCorrelated(). Every correlated column must have depth 1 (expr.binder->correlated_columns).
(2) Peel the subquery plan (expr.subquery.plan): optional LogicalProjections, then a LogicalAggregate with no groups and exactly one BoundAggregateExpression. That aggregate must be min or max, without DISTINCT, filter or ORDER BY, and its child must be a column ref. Below it: optional projections and LogicalFilter(s) over LOGICAL_CROSS_PRODUCT / LogicalGet leaves only. Bail on anything else: joins with conditions, subqueries in the subquery, limits.
(3) The outer root must likewise be a tree of cross products, gets and filters; collect its gets and its conjuncts (the outer WHERE conjuncts are in `condition`, since the FROM is unfiltered at this point).
(4) Match each subquery LogicalGet to a distinct outer LogicalGet on the same table (GetTable() pointer equal, both with empty table_filters, no dynamic filters or parameters). Build a binding map from subquery bindings to outer bindings via column_ids and the projection map; bail if a referenced column is missing in the outer get. Map correlated BoundColumnRef (depth 1) to the outer binding it names.
(5) Every remapped subquery conjunct must Equals() some outer conjunct. The unmatched outer conjuncts, other than the subquery conjunct, must reference only columns of unmatched (extra) outer gets. Every correlated column must belong to an extra get and must appear in a matched COMPARE_EQUAL conjunct, which rejects NULLs. Nothing may be volatile, and no other conjunct may hold a subquery.
(6) Rewrite: root = LogicalFilter(all conjuncts except the subquery one) over root. Then add LogicalWindow(new table index) with a BoundWindowExpression of type WINDOW_AGGREGATE, using the same aggregate function bound to the remapped argument, partitions = the outer correlated column refs, default frame (whole partition: no ORDER BY, so RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING covers it). Replace the condition with `colref = BoundColumnRef(window output)`, keeping the original comparison orientation and any cast. Copy how window expressions are built in src/planner/binder/query_node/plan_select_node.cpp / bind_window_expression for LogicalWindow construction.
If any check fails, leave everything untouched (the existing decorrelation path). Test against the original by running q02 with different p_size/type/region values. Add a sqllogic-style check with a case where the extra table has duplicate keys (min is unaffected) and with NULL correlated keys.
expected_gain: q02: about -20% (47 to about 36-38ms hot, measured with a hand rewrite). Possibly more, since the CTE materialisation also disappears.
generality: Any query with a correlated MIN/MAX scalar subquery whose FROM/WHERE is a subset of the outer query's join, for example 'rows achieving the per-group min/max' (argmin-style) patterns, TPC-H Q2-like supplier/price queries and latest-record lookups. Queries not matching the strict pattern are unchanged. A possible slowdown is a very large outer join result with a single huge partition, where the window (which materialises and partitions) could cost more than the delim plus hash aggregate. Mitigation: only MIN/MAX, and the outer result has to be built anyway.
risk: Medium-high in correctness, low in performance. The pattern checks must be strict: the same tables, an exact conjunct subset after remapping, extra-table conjuncts only on extra tables, correlated columns NULL-rejected by an equality, MIN/MAX only. Binding remap bugs show up as wrong results, so validate with several parameterisations and with EXPLAIN. The implementation is moderately large (about 250-400 lines).

title: Avoid wide string payload cost on hash-join build side (late materialisation of build payload)
hypothesis: Hot: the q02 outer join returning only numeric and short columns runs in about 20ms. Adding s_address, s_phone and s_comment (20k-row supplier build side) gives about 30ms, while the scan of those columns alone is about 2ms. The cost seems to be in HT build/gather and TopN of the wide strings, but the measurement was noisy (±5ms).
plan: Profile first. If it is confirmed, consider carrying the row id on the build side and fetching the wide payload after the TopN. Not ready to dispatch.
generality: Join plus TopN queries projecting wide strings from a dimension
